utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Good morning, everybody. Could you the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Accused Miletic is not present today. Madam Fauveau, we've been informed that a waiver will be coming in due course. Do you confirm that from your knowledge at least?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can safely proceed, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much. On the Prosecution side, I see Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Elderkin. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Nikolic on the Beara Defence team, and then I think it's just Mr. Haynes. All right. Good morning, to you Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're still testifying pursuant to the solemn declaration that you entered last week, so you don't need to repeat it. Mr. Ostojic will take matters up from where he left them when you were last here. Mr. Ostojic, good morning to you, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you. Before we begin, if I could respond quickly to the Honourable Judge Kwon's question of last week as to where the column appears, and just so everyone can follow. The column that I was referring to was reflected on the document in e-court, which was marked as 2D553, and it has the doc number of 2D41-0042, and I apologise again for that confusion to the Court and to Judge Kwon. And I looked at that, and it was not in the second, which is his initial report filed in October or prepared in October. But it is in there, so if I may proceed. Secondly, the Court requested to identify the witnesses which do have pseudonyms and those who don't, and we had did identify that there were four that had pseudonyms, so we will attempt at least for our purposes to go through the witnesses with the proper names. I will need at this time, though, to provide Professor Wagenaar with a copy of this little list of names so that he could follow them because his report actually at certain times doesn't contain the specific name but only the number. I've distributed to the court officer as well as to my learned friends from the Prosecution as well as from the Defence this one sheet of paper, so if I'm permitted to tender that to the witness, it may assist us with some of the direct and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May I do so, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I note that you're writing a couple of the numbers and names down?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I enter them in my table for as far as I didn't have them, so I will not unwantingly use the wrong names. I'm almost done. Right. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, and just so the record's clear, we've also asked you to provide any notes or other documentation that you have so that the Prosecution may take a look at it, and this morning we met with the Prosecutor prior to your testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you gave the Prosecution, I think, a -- two pages of some notes that you've maintained in handwriting, which was in English, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And he's returned to you the original, and both the Prosecution and I have a copy of that, and in due course we may file it with the Court and distribute it to the parties. If it's necessary, we can do it at the next break. So if I may proceed. Professor, last Wednesday, I believe, we were discussing the difference between identification and recognition. Can you share with us, why does the difference exist in testing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us why, if at all, does a distinction or difference exist in testing both identification and recognition of persons?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Recognition -- the term "recognition" is used for people who encounter someone, as I used to say, at the scene of the crime who they already know beforehand. Whether or not that claim is true cannot be tested by a psychological test; and later on, it would be useless to confront such a witness with a lineup because that lineup would show one person they have known for a long time and other persons they've never seen at all. It would be very easy for them to identify this one person they know, and it doesn't prove that they met this person at the scene of the crime, so that would be a meaningless test. Identification is used in this Tribunal for the situation where a witness encountered someone, let's say again at the scene of the crime, but that was the first time in their life. And if it was also the last time in their life, it can be tested whether this person is the same as one of the accused by having the accused in a lineup with other foils. And now if the witness is able to identify this one person in the lineup, that proves the likelihood that he have seen this person before, and, as I said, if the only possible occasion where they met is at the scene of the crime, then this localises, this places the accused at the scene of the crime, so that would be a meaningful test. The implication of that is that if the accused claims that he was never at the scene of the crime, then the identification might be a falsification of that claim; and therefore, it's a very, very important test to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now -- and thank you. Professor, help me understand. What are the standards or the tests that would be utilized in order to determine or assess if a witness under the category of recognition is examining or called upon to give a recollection of that which he purportedly saw. So sticking with the category recognition, what are the tests that may be utilized? And you've told us about identification. Which is the foils and, as I call it, the photo board. But let's stick for the time being with witnesses that fall under the category of recognition.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of recognition, there are two important things to consider. One is, if the witness claims this was a person already familiar to him, then it must be investigated what the nature of this familiarity is, when they met before and how the witness came to know the name and the outer appearance of this person. And second, when they encountered at the scene of the crime, it must be established what actually the conditions for an accurate perception were. The most important aspect of these conditions are distance and lighting, at what distance did he see this person, and what were the light conditions. And obviously, if the distance is too long or the light is too poor, he would not be able to see very well the outer appearance of the persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are there certain recognised standards in determining whether or not distance may be considered too long or too far?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, just an objection and more of a question. There's not one word in the report I received about standard tests for recognition witnesses. There is not one word in the report about standards for light and distance, and I don't know why if this is expert testimony which he's inquiring of it was not included in the report, which was begun over a year ago. There are references in the report to saying, well, lighting's important, whether the witness could see is important, but there's not one word about standard tests. I'm not aware of these tests, and I don't know why that hasn't been provided to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, would you like to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think my learned friend needs to read the report a little more carefully. I think that those tests as he's cited in his footnotes and articles which we provided are quite universally known, and I think the Professor does in fact cite to them in our report, as we're going to go through it, I hope, with certain witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the use of the word "test" that is the confusing element here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I said standards or tests, but if I didn't, it was just trying to use a different one. It's the standards that are utilized in connection with recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There are citations -- I'm not going to try to stop the testimony, Your Honour, but there are citations, two articles. That is not the same as an expert report giving his opinion on these conditions on the test, just having -- there are let's of citations that are not included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That may be true, Mr. Nicholls. However, I recollect quite vividly when the witness was testifying last week that he explained the standards that have been arrived at over the years and that they are pretty much standard throughout the world. I mean, whether they are standards as such or a test as such, he was, of course, referring to the manner in which recognition ought to be conducted. I don't know. I mean, Professor, before we decide, do you think you can provide us with an insight on the basis of the objection and what would be your reaction to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. On page 3 of my report, I described that investigating the claims of a familiar person should be by what I call a thorough analysis of the conditions in which the observation took place. It's in the second linear on page 3, and I think I was going to refer to what this thorough analysis entails and, of course, logically the perception of a person at a certain -- in a certain situation, whether he's familiar or not familiar firstly depends on the perceptual conditions, and the decision for the witness that this is a familiar person or an unfamiliar person logically comes after the perception of that person. So for the two situations, familiar or unfamiliar, the perception of a person at the screen of the crime is exactly the same and doesn't have to be described twice in the report. And that's why I only said a thorough analysis of the conditions and, of course, these conditions are the same as in the case of an unfamiliar person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I don't want to belabour the point, but the rules for lineups are very clearly stated in his report, and the standards are set forth for this separate topic that is absent. There's the reference to it, but there's no description of minimum distances, lighting, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, but what's it going to change? I think there is a question, and the professor can either answer it or not answer it. And he has answered it in any case, I mean, as far as I'm concerned. I don't know that there's further information that he could give us. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in the process of answering it, and I started with describing the factor distance, the significance of the factor distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, please. Go ahead, and proceed with answering the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, the two most important factors for judging the perceptual condition are distance and illumination [Realtime transcript read in error, "elimination"], and I cited two of my own publications, which both are studies on the ability of people to perceive faces of other people at various distances and under various illumination conditions. There are two publications: One is on familiar people; the other is on unfamiliar people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, excuse me. Let me just stop you because in the record it says "elimination," but I think you're talking about illumination, which is lighting. Am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just on two instances, I notice that we had a hard time hearing you.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it's distance and illumination?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Illumination, with an I. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could just proceed.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will. And the bottom line of these two publications is that the difficulties of perceiving other people are independent of familiarity or unfamiliarity; the outcomes are the same. That also answers, I think, the question of the Prosecution, why did I not discuss them for both situations separately? Well, actually, they are the same. That's not only a logical conclusion. It's also based on my empirical research.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is there a specific guideline as to what that is in terms of fixed measurements such as metres when we discuss distances?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. What my research shows is that at distances from 0 to about 12 metres, there is no problem of perceiving other people. At 20 metres, in my studies it has dropped considerably and -- which means that -- which does not mean that you cannot recognise people at 20 metres, but the probability of an error increases rapidly at those distances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what would you call the area from 12 to 20 metres?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 12 to 20 is -- that is where doubt starts to rise. Beyond 20, it definitely is a very risky thing to accept a recognition; below 12, it's quite safe; and in between, risk starts to rise. There's no sharp demarcation line, but between 12 and 20, that's where the problem starts to rise. I can't help it that there are no very strict conditions, but science is just like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor, what about other factors in determining or testing this recognition category of witnesses that we'll get into specifically. Are there other factors that one would inquire such as the height or other descriptive characteristics in order to assess whether persons who fall within the category of recognition should be deemed reliable in the evidence that they're attempting to put forward?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned height, but I think height comes in later. The -- after illumination and distance, the thing you need to consider is how much time did the witness have to observe that person? Was that in, say, a flash, or was it, say, many minutes or maybe hours? From which aspect did the witness see that person, only from behind or only from the side? As you may remember, if you see a person only from the side whereas most photo boards contain pictures from the front, that might be extremely difficult for a witness to do. So it's important whether he could see that person in the face, from the side, or only from behind. Was the witness in a quiet condition to make observations or, as in the Kupreskic case, was the witness trying to escape and running? And then an important factor appears to be, was the witness already expecting to see a certain person, because that might make it more easy at a distance or in low illumination conditions to see what you expect instead to see what is really present. So expectation is clearly important. Now, you mentioned height, and maybe I can answer that question a little bit broader. In people's descriptions, and usually they are interrogated about that, there's usually mention of how tall was that person, what was his build, how heavy was he, and how old was he? And clearly if you perceive a person, you can't see exactly how tall he is in centimetres or inches. You cannot see exactly how old he is or how much kilograms or pounds he weighs. So when you ask witnesses to answer such questions, you ask them to guess, to make estimates about something they could not actually see. And I myself use as a rule that if they make these guesses they can easily be 5 centimetres off, 5 kilograms off, and 5 years off. You should not be surprised if the error is double of that, so occasionally it can also be 10 centimetres off, 10 kilograms off, 10 years off. If the discrepancy between what the witness says and the person he allegedly saw is more than 10 centimetres, more than 10 kilograms, more than 10 years, then you should start to consider the alternative, which is that he saw a different person because beyond 10, that shady area starts where there is doubt about whether he saw the alleged person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what's the area that we would call from the 5, whether it's 5 centimetres, 5 kilos, or 5 years to the 10 centimetres, 10 kilos, and 10 years? Is that also a grey area, or that's where you have some doubt, or explain further, if you will.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, between 5 and 10, you find repeatedly -- I've seen many cases, and -- it's not an absolute exception to be between 5 and 10 off on those three dimensions. So there is no good reason to say -- to conclude, that witness must be talking about a different person. Beyond 10, it becomes a hypothesis worth investigating, whether this was a different person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you for that. I know we covered, now, the height, weight, and age, at least briefly. But let's go back to the one you've considered to be a factor that's important after distance and illumination, and that, sir, was when you said time, time to observe. Now, what's the significance of that, if you could share with us your understanding, and I think we can logically assert or we can come up with our own standard or understanding of it, but from your experience what is the standard for time to observe?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, time is only an indication of something that is psychologically important, which is attention. If you see a lot of people passing by and one particular person is visible for a few seconds, there's no absolute guarantee that you pay attention to that person at all. And if you do not pay attention, you do not properly perceive, and consequently, no information is stored in your memory. If you meet a person, on the other hand, for several hours, you talk to him, attention cannot be a problem. You must have paid attention to this person, which means you had all opportunity to see him and commit the information about his appearance into your memory. So time in itself doesn't tell us very much, but time leads us to attention. Now, the thing is that most witnesses are able to report how much time it was, so that's good question to ask. But as a psychologist, it is significant to me because time tells me something about attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So help me understand this: Based upon a reasonable degree of certainty, the lower time a witness who is considered in this category as recognition spends with an individual that he's purporting to identify, what's the significance of that versus the greater amount of time such a person under this recognition category spends with an individual? Is there a variance or a difference just as a matter of time? For example, the more time you would spend someone, can we conclude that the more likelihood that you will recall that person, or the less time or a fleeting glance at someone may or may not be considered relevant? Help us with that.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. If you talk about a fleeing glance, there are some countries where some fleeing glance testimony even is forbidden because it's notoriously dangerous to show that if you saw a person in a fleeing glance that you really stored into your memory what this person looked like. The situation where you have a conversation with the person, that's not at all a fleeing glance, and then in a conversation you must look at one another, so you cannot fail to note the appearance. I'm not saying that you could not perceive people in a fleeing glance. I'm also -- I'm only saying that it becomes increasingly risky to assume an accurate perception of a person when the time of perception gets very short. It becomes risky because the likelihood that you had an accurate perception is decreasing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's -- if we can move on and look at some of the rule, and we touched upon a couple of them last week, but I wanted to ask you, you mention in Rule number 2, "unconscious transference." And if you could just put that in better perspective for us. I think I understand it, but I still may need your assistance in that regard.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unconscious transference is -- occurs in a lineup where the supposition is that the accused shown among foils in the lineup is either never seen by the witness or seen at the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So this would be --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The risk is that the witness actually saw this accused in a different place, not at the scene of the crime but somewhere else, maybe on a billboard or when he was travelling in the train and sat opposite him. If the witness does not realise that he saw this person at another place but, in fact, when he looks at the photo board realises that only one of these people looks familiar, he may point at that person and add in words, this is the person I saw at the scene of the crime, and what unconsciously the witness is doing - and that's why it's called unconscious transference - is transfer the encounter he forgot about, the billboard or in the train, to the scene of the crime. Now the witness thinks he looks familiar because I saw him at the scene of the crime. So one condition for photo board, photo lineup testing is that it must be absolutely certain that there is no other possible place where the witness could have seen the accused apart from that one encounter at the scene of the crime described in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But just so I have a better appreciation for it, since we are -- and I want to make sure we all understand is we're talking about identification in that category as opposed to recognition. What occurs, if anything, if a Prosecutor or investigator with the Prosecution would show a witness who falls within the category of identification other photographs, although not a photo board, but photographs or videos of a proposed person that they claim to have seen? What effect if any does it have on that person's statement, and I think you touch upon it on your rule, but you used the word "irrelevant." I'm directing your attention to, actually, the first full paragraph of your report, and it's the very last word in that paragraph. And I understood it to be - and I'll let you answer it - to be unreliable, but can you share with us your thoughts on that and your opinions?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, now, you ask me a very complicated question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it is one question, but let me try to answer it. What I said is that the witness may absolutely be honest when he says, I believe that I met this person at the scene of the crime, and that's why I'm able to identify him in the photo board. If actually the witness saw this person somewhere else but forgot it, you may ask the person, are you sure you did not see this person in another place? An honest witness might answer, yes, I'm sure, I never saw him at any other place; and still, he might be wrong about that. So it does not really help to ask witnesses who take part in photo board identification tests whether they are certain that they met this person at the scene of the crime and no one else. Although this is an absolute condition for running the test, you cannot verify whether this is the case by just asking the witness. You should investigate the situation in another way. For instance, in the previous case in which I testified, the case was that one of the accused had been running for a political office, so his face might have become known to people just by looking at the television or looking at billboards. Now, witnesses may have forgotten that and now believe they know this face because they saw this person commit criminal acts. But by just asking them, are you sure you never saw this face in a different place, that is not the right way to solve that problem. You must in the investigation yourself certify that this person had never been made visible to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it does, and I apologise that it was perhaps compound, but I want to stick with unconscious transference. How can we make a determination, or can we, of whether or not a witness who falls within the category of identification actually underwent an unconscious transference?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, logically the situation is that investigations can never exclude the logical possibility that there was another encounter. I would say only God knows that. But on the other hand, investigation may bring to the surface those other situations, and then the answer is given. To give you an example, if during the investigation and prior to the photo board testing the investigators themselves showed pictures of the accused to the witness, then we know that there has been this type of prior encounter, and therefore, the photo board identification test should be excluded. So I'm not saying investigation can guarantee that an encounter did not take place; but on the other hand, investigation sometimes reveal that the encounter did take place. That's the relevant thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just -- let's try to make a practical application at least to this rule. I know you're going to have to utilize Rule number 5, but I'd like to discuss Mr. Egbers for a minute. I think if you recall his testimony, and I know you have your notes there, but for the purpose of moving it along he was a member of DutchBat, I think, as we all know. And keeping in mind this unconscious transference, if you remember his testimony, was he asked by the investigators to give a description, or was he simply shown videos seven to eight times which fit a general description of what he purported to see, and then tell me if that rule that you have, among others, were violated within connection with the testimony that the Prosecution was proffering with that witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Professor. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was a little bit leading, and I'm going to start objecting to leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Really, they should look at the question. I don't think it was. If you really look at it, it's a fair question. I'm not directing him saying the Prosecution did make that mistake. It's in his report, but I'll ask the question in a very simple and straightforward manner so we don't have many more interruptions. So I will restate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you review the testimony of a gentleman by the name of Mr. Egbers?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us which if any category under your analysis with his testimony with respect to identification or recognition fall under?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. My notes say that the witness, Mr. Egbers, said that he was once introduced to Mr. Beara. That was the first time he met him, so that was at that time not a familiar person. It was an unknown person to him. Mr. Egbers said Beara introduced himself, and Egbers also added that he did not pay much attention; he saw him only a few minutes. So that to my mind would be an ideal situation to apply a photo identification test --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because two things: One, he was unknown to him, so he could pass positively the photo identification test only if the person he saw was really Mr. Beara; then he might identify him in the test. The second thing is, his statement leaves some room for doubt. He said it was very short; I did not pay much attention. So there might be a question, whom did he actually see? The person introduced himself as Beara, but later he also said, I saw a giant colonel who might have been Beara. So that uncertainty can be resolved by asking him to take part in a photo test, and say -- from my point of view, I would say, and that solves it. If he is able to identify him, that makes it very likely he actually saw Mr. Beara. If he is not, we don't know whom he met. We know for sure he doesn't have a very accurate memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did the investigators to the best of your knowledge having reviewed the documents that were presented to you conduct a photo identification board with witness Egbers?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did they conduct any sort of identification process to show them any photographs or videos?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my notes say that he was shown a video, no photos, and that video was a very short video of an actual event and, of course, the scene taken was never organised to constitute a fair lineup. There were no foils all fitting the same description. So that video, I don't know exactly which purpose it served. It's not for me to decide why it was done, but I can state that that video, showing the video cannot come in the place of, say, a proper lineup identification test.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, do you, Professor, recall how many times the Prosecution showed this short video to Mr. Egbers?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know how often -- that's your question, how often he showed the video? This was a very short video, but I have no notes how often it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What if in his testimony Mr. Egbers says that he was shown the video seven to eight times before he can make an assessment as to whether or not that may be the person he purportedly saw, and I think we could find that specifically as I've given it to my learned friend in the transcript, page 2850.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, yeah, yeah. I see that this -- it was seven or eight times, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think if you glance at your table that you have --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- you may be able to be assisted with having that information and highlighting it for us, in fact.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, showing it once or eight times in my perspective does not change my opinion that such a video can never come in the place of a photo lineup, but if your question is, what does it mean if Mr. Egbers could even in the video not identify anyone until he saw it seven or eight times, I must say it's very hard to say what that means because then you need a very accurate description of that situation. I must expand a little bit on that. The situation of a photo lineup test is very much standardised. We know exactly how it must be done, what is said, how often things are shown, and the record also usually reflect the actual proceedings. So there's no doubt about what happened. If you start to see -- to show videos or photos according to another protocol, then we suddenly -- we don't know what actually happened. So in this case I would want to know, why did they show it seven or eight times? Did they say, we'll show you, it's very short, don't respond, we'll show you it a couple of times so you can see better, and is the reason that -- did he not respond was he was told not to respond; or did he say after the first time, don't recognise anyone, and then they said, we'll show you again, and up to eight times, he said I don't -- so those proceedings must be very explicit before an expert can say anything about it. In this case, I've not followed up that aspect of the file and of Egbers' testimony because to me the most important thing is, Mr. Egbers did not participate in a proper photo lineup test whether to my mind he would have been an ideal witness to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, and I know we're discussing the rules as well as trying to make a practical application to some of the testimony as you've done, but I'm just trying to focus this portion of your testimony in giving your answer. How significant or important is it to properly construct and to prepare questions that you would ask a witness that falls under the identification category such as Mr. Egbers, and I would direct your attention, Professor, to your own Rule number 5. And I believe that's the one that's applicable, and you can tell me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. This, I think, is very much related to what I said, which is the photo -- the proper photo lineup test is very well defined. The instructions given to the witness have been studied all over the world, and we very much agree about what a witness should be told and what the witness should not be told. The witness should first have described a certain person, and then the question in the photo lineup -- subsequent photo lineup test is, this person you just described, is he present in this photo lineup test, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do we know, Professor, what those questions were that the Prosecution was asking Mr. Egbers in particular?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm not aware of an accurate recording, and I'm not surprised because showing a video is also not a proper and well organised photo lineup test where the instructions to the witness are clear. So for instance, to give you an example, one of the most important aspects of instructions in a photo lineup test is that you tell the witness, do not guess. If you do not recognise someone immediately, do not try to guess. Only point at one of these people if you are certain that you recognise them. Now, if you show someone a video with the question, do you recognise anyone here, at least the witness should have been told, do not guess, and that should have been recorded, the instructions. We know that the proportion of false identifications raises dramatically if this very simple sentence "do not guess" is omitted from the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Professor, I'm really looking when we discuss this witness Egbers, you mentioned in your report, and I know we're jumping ahead a little bit, but I think it might be an easier way to proceed. And if you could look on your -- I think it's page -- the section where you say "other attempts at identification," which follows part 2 of your table, and it's under section 3. And you, although, discuss two other witnesses that the Prosecution has called, Babic and Erdemovic, as well as Mr. Egbers, within that section you highlight, I think, for us that there were several rules that were violated in your opinion in connection with the procedure and process that the Prosecution and its investigators utilized for purposes of identification, which include Egbers. We've talked about Rule number 5. Sticking with Mr. Egbers, what other rules do you see with respect to the testimony that was proffered were violated?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you go -- and you're relating to showing a video to Mr. Egbers, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if I may add, given that we just discussed -- to be fair to the Prosecution, given also the questions that they may have formulated because you looked at the transcript, and the Prosecution I think as reflected in the transcript told the witness that they were investigating a person by the name of Beara.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So given that, although we know now from you the significance of that as well as the video, can you share with us what other rules were violated?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah. If the situation was that Mr. Egbers claimed to have met the accused Mr. Beara only once, not before that encounter and not after, that at least the conditions for a lineup test are fulfilled. The only question then is, showing a video, does it qualify as a lineup test? There's a second condition, which is Mr. Egbers should have given a description of the person he saw which is detailed enough to choose foils that fit the same description. So Rule 3 may be relevant in as far as it's not absolutely certain that Egbers gave an accurate description of the person he saw. Rule 4 was violated because other people shown in this video clearly were no foils in the sense that they were chosen according to the description given by Mr. Egbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, would we call that a suggestive type of video? You mentioned it, and help me understand what a suggestive photo board is.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. A suggestive photo board is a photo board where, actually, only one person is shown who fits the description just given by the witness, and the others do not fit that description, so automatically the attention of the witness will be focused upon that one photo. And that's a highly suggestive situation because then if the witness has only the slightest tendency to guess, he will point at this only person who fits the description. So Rule 5 is relevant, as we said, because we don't know what the instructions were; they must be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, just so we are all following --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that's my reason to say such a showing of a television -- a televised event, that is not at all the same as showing a well-constructed photo lineup.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, let's turn to the witness Erdemovic who we touched upon last week, showing you -- I think it was a stipulation with the 1st of May, 2007, with another accused in this case where they did show a photo board. I'm not going to ask you whether that photo board was proper, but the witness in that case and the Prosecution have agreed he was not able to be depicted. There was another stipulation, though, that I believe that you read, and it's reflected in the materials that you reviewed, and it involved Mr. Beara and that witness, Erdemovic. Do you remember, sir, that material that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the photograph that was shown to Mr. Erdemovic, do you have any opinions as to whether or not that photograph with -- to help you recall, with five individuals in it, it was not a photo board necessarily, but that photograph shown to the witness, was that highly suggestive?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That was a photo, and I think that's the photo we were shown in the previous session where you see one colonel sitting among a number of much younger other military people. The rank of this colonel can be seen. There's one person who is older. Not only that, there's one person who is clearly the leader by the way he sits, and he takes much of the space. It's clear that no simpleton military person would do that and push away his own colonel. So it must be clear to everyone who sees this photo for the first time, if the question is, who's in charge here, who's the colonel, that was only one person who qualify because of the way he sits, because of his insignia, and because he is much older than the others. So if that is how the witness also described the person he saw, a colonel who is in charge, who is older than normal soldiers, who might be in his 50s or so, then that photo shows -- reveals exactly the aspect of a suggestive lineup, which is, does only one person fit in the description?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me understand this: Why would the Prosecution or its investigators in this particular circumstance with this witness Erdemovic provide a photo board with one of the accused and not provide a photo board with respect to Mr. Beara? Now, we all know from that stipulation that Erdemovic did not identify Mr. Beara, even though the photograph was highly suggestive or suggestive at the very least, but why would the Prosecution do you think not prepare a proper photo board with respect to this witness?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no way to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer. Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He answered it. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, help me understand this, Professor. With respect to this witness Mr. Erdemovic and the one photo board that -- although I know you didn't analyse it to determine whether it was proper, you looked at the photograph which bear Mrs. Beara. Do you know the significance of showing a type of photographer that was shown to Mr. Erdemovic where it depicts in a highly suggestive manner who the person was? What significance may that have on someone's recollection or in this unconscious transference that we were previously discussing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer that question, Professor. Reference previous page, line 20. Before I intervened, there should be in the transcript the witness's beginning of an answer. I recollect him saying, "There is no way I could know that." That does not show in the transcript, and it's important because otherwise Mr. Nicholls intervention doesn't make sense. Yes, Professor. You could answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not certain I understand your question correctly, but there's one important thing to say about showing Mr. -- the witness Erdemovic this photograph. Mr. Erdemovic was also a witness who met -- who says, who stated he met a person this far unknown to him. So Mr. Erdemovic, his statement could be further tested by asking him to participate in a photo lineup test. But after he saw this one picture in which Mr. Beara is featured, and I think there is -- although I have no way to assess it was Mr. Beara. I assume that's the supposition underlying your question. If he was shown a picture of Mr. Beara, from there on Mr. Erdemovic cannot take part into a proper photo lineup any more, which means just by showing him a photograph for whatever purpose that I cannot fathom, I think, you lost the opportunity of really testing him, so there is a price of showing photographs to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So would there be any significance to a subsequent preparation of a photo board showing a witness like Erdemovic given what we know, that he was shown this other photograph that would be considered suggestive?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the risk would be that if later on you ask Mr. Erdemovic to take part into a proper photo lineup, that indeed one of the persons shown to him would look familiar, and he would not realise that it was because he saw him in a photograph, and if he really had forgotten that, he might now claim, this is the person I met before, whereas in fact it is the person he saw in the photograph. That would be an example of unconscious transference, and that's exactly why you either should not show photographs to witnesses who are still expected to take part in photo lineups; or conversely, that's exactly why after you have shown photos line -- photos, you should decide -- you should exclude this witness further from photo lineups. Now, that's actually what happens. I am not criticizing that. Mr. Erdemovic did not take part in photo lineups, so nothing has caused wrong there, although I think from the viewpoint of investigation it could have been very useful to ask him to take part in a photo lineup.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's direct our attention to this third individual that you highlight in your report, which we've initially marked as 122, which is Babic. With respect to that, did the photo -- did the Prosecution violate any rules in connection with their attempts to have Mr. Babic make an identification?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, from my notes at least, Mr. Babic claimed that he met with a person this far unknown to him. He says he saw a lieutenant-colonel but didn't know who exactly that colonel was, so he met a person with a certain rank. So, also, Mr. Babic would be an ideal witness to take part in the photo lineup because he never saw this person before, there's doubt about whom he actually met, and that question can be solved by a proper photo lineup. He gave a description: blond, thin hair, short -- short hair at the back, and a receding hairline, no mustache, no glasses. That really leaves room for many different people, and since in the pictures I have seen of Mr. Beara there were always glasses, the positive mentioning of no glasses, not just leaving out glasses, but explicitly mentioning I saw no glasses even increases the doubts about whom he actually saw and makes it, therefore, the more relevant to test him in a photo lineup. He saw a tall, strong, heavily built person in his 50s. Then he was shown pictures, a number of pictures, and he didn't recognise anyone in those pictures. Now, the significance to me is that from there on, from the moment he was shown pictures supposedly also featuring Mr. Beara, Babic could not be tested in a photo lineup anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So what is --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he did not recognise anyone in the pictures is more difficult for me to interpret because whether he should have recognised Mr. Beara in these pictures if he really met him at all also depends, of course, on the quality of the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Were there any other -- and I call them lost opportunities, but you can tell us what it is. But were there any other lost opportunities where the Prosecution had where they could have simply with this photo identification board or -- and any other manner that you've suggested preserve and capture such testimony with respect to identification other than these three individuals where the identification tests were improper? So with the exclusion of Babic, Erdemovic, and Egbers, were there other instances?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The logical situation is this: My table on page 9 lists 12 witnesses. Three witnesses are categorized as familiar; nine are categorized as unknown. So in principle, those nine could have been tested in a photo lineup. Now, I wrote at the top of page 10 that probably numbers 152 - that's PW 162 - and number 131 - that's Mr. Peric - should not have been tested because after their encounter they might have had another opportunity to meet or see Mr. Beara, and that violates one of the conditions. There must be either no encounter or, at the most, one. And that leaves seven witnesses who could have been tested, and the two you mentioned, Mr. Babic and Mr. Erdemovic, are only two out of these seven. That leaves five who have not been tested. Now, I'm not in the position to order identification testing. The only thing I could have said is that the statements made by these witnesses, the reliability of those statements could be much -- much easier be judged if we also had the outcomes of proper identification tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. And just so we're clear, we actually discussed three, sir, not just that Erdemovic and Babic, but --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also Egbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- also Egbers, correct. I just want to make sure the record's clear. And also, you mentioned one of the witnesses Peric, P-E-R-I-C, as -- his given number as we've known it from time to time was 131. I just wanted to make sure that's clear on the transcript. Let's proceed and talk about -- at least for a few moments about recognition again. With respect to recognition, you've categorised how many witness that would fall into that category for purposes of your and our assessment?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are three who claimed that they met with the person they saw before, so that was to them a familiar person, which logically implies that their claims cannot be tested by a lineup, photo board procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so that I'm following you, in that instance a photo identification board is not indicated or is not something that we would need, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It might even be misleading because they might find it easy to identify Mr. Beara in a photo board because they knew him anyway, and it doesn't prove they met Mr. Beara at the place that they described. And for any person not being totally aware of the difference between familiar and unknown people, such people might believe that the photo board proves the reliability of their statements, but it doesn't. Therefore, presenting photo board identification for familiar witnesses I would say is undesirable, is not helpful to the Court, and is misleading those others who are not aware of the distinction between the two categories.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned these three individuals that fall within this recognition category, who are familiar -- who were purportedly familiar with Mr. Beara, I say "purportedly," and we'll address one in particular. Just so that you follow me correctly, just -- the three individuals is a person by the name of Bircakovic, Celanovic, and the third one, Professor, just so that we're focussed, does have a pseudonym, and he's been identified as PW 161, so with respect --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With respect to this third individual, we will not be referencing his name, but we'll follow and identify him simply for our purposes as PW 161. Were you able to review -- are those the three individuals that fall within that category of familiar and recognition that we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the three.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So that we can see the parameters of your testimony a little more clear, the balance of the witnesses, under which category would they fall on or under?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not getting your question. Can you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You have shared with us the category of identification and witnesses who are unfamiliar and only had an encounter purportedly with Mr. Beara. We discussed three. You identified 7 out of those 12. I want to go through what other categories there are. We've now identified a second category that we call recognition. Within that category you have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do very much apologise again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to walk you through it hopefully slower so that we can understand it. You have this category of witness of who have purportedly recognised or are familiar with Mr. Beara. I think we have three of them in that category, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We've highlighted in part the testimony with respect to witnesses who have not -- or were not familiar with Mr. Beara and who purportedly have seen him and the flaws if you will of not preparing a proper photo identification board. Is there any other category other than this one, or is this the last one, the recognition with these three individuals that we may discuss?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you're still referring to the 12 witnesses in my table, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can split them up in the following manner: Three claimed familiarity, so they cannot be tested in the photo lineup.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And those are the --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nine claimed that they saw an unfamiliar person, which leaves in principle nine to be tested in a photo lineup. But two of them should be excluded because they might have a later encounter. That leaves seven, and of those seven we have discussed three, and that leaves four others who also could have been tested in the photo lineup.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so we have a complete record, those four others, and I apologise very much for leading on this issue, but I think we know that it's PW 165, it was Mr. Boering; PW 104; and a witness by the name of Milosevic, which is under number 126. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you glean from the record with respect to those four who were not shown a photo board, did you glean from the record any understanding or appreciation as to why the Prosecution or its investigators did not with respect to these four witnesses show them a photo identification board?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid we are coming very close to a question that we've had a couple of minutes before, which is, would I know why the investigators and the Prosecution do certain things; and I would say it's not my task to know that. I did not find an explicit statement declaring why it would have been undesirable for any of these witnesses to do that, nor why it would be absolutely physically impossible to do that. And there are such conditions, like if a witness says I met with Mr. Beara but then gives a description of Mr. Beara which is so far off that choosing foils in accordance with this description would immediately make the lineup biased because then all foils would resemble another person and not Mr. Beara, in that case there would be a good logical reason for not testing this witness in the photo lineup, which doesn't mean you have to discard that witness. It only means it cannot be tested in a photo lineup. But I did not see, if that's the question, for the seven witnesses who qualified but were not tested such a reason in the records that I could also follow why, then, they were not further tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And all I was asking, and forgive me if it sounded like a similar question, I was just curious to know from your review of the documents that you received whether you found any reason that the Prosecution may have given us or anyone as to why they didn't, so I'm not asking you to speculate. But let's go now, turn to this recognition category with the three witness. The first witness we'd like to look at if we may is Mr. Bircakovic, which is 142, and I think you in your report after part 2 -- it's under paragraph in bold number 4. Do you see that, and just so everyone can follow along with us, and I believe it's on page 10.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, what's your question about Mr. Bircakovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to make sure we're on it.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to this witness, sir, are the conditions upon which the witness claims to have seen Mr. Beara relevant in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bircakovic did not positively say he saw Mr. Beara at a certain place, a well known person to him. He said he may have seen him, but he was not certain who he saw. Well, that's a logical problem. If you first claim familiarity and you meet a familiar person at a certain place, then in principle you're also quite certain whom you've met because it's a familiar person. If you meet a person who you call familiar but you are not actually certain who that is, then maybe you should question the familiarity, and this makes it very difficult to categorise this particular witness in one or the other categories, which makes it for me also extremely difficult to say what the proper way of testing this witness should be. Why he wasn't certain whom he had met can depend -- can be the result of that he wasn't so familiar or that Mr. Beara was very familiar but the actual viewing conditions were very bad, so he couldn't see who that was. There are so many possibilities that I would be forced to guess at what's happened here, and it's not my task to guess. I can only say this makes it a very difficult to understand witness from my respect. There's nothing I could do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we look at your paragraph number 4 on your report.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And help me understand this sentence, although to keep it in context I may have to read the preceding sentence. It says: "For the three witnesses who were already familiar with Beara, no formal identification test can be held." You proceed, Professor, stating -- this is where I have the question, so just bear with me: "The only thing that can be judged is whether the conditions described by them would allow a reliable recognition." Further, with respect to this witness in particular, you state: "For Witness number 142, this seems not to be the case, as he was not even certain that he met with Mr. Beara."

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What were -- how do you reach this opinion, if you could tell me what the basis is for this opinion.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the same as I just said. If he knows Mr. Beara, then he meets him but isn't certain that is Mr. Beara, then one explanation of that is that the perceptual conditions, the conditions for viewing this person were so bad that you cannot trust his statement about it. But another logical explanation is that although he says Mr. Beara was familiar to me, in fact, he was not. So you also have to consider the basis on which he claims this familiarity. If it had been his neighbour for 25 years, you can trust he is familiar. But there is not so much information in the file about on what grounds he declares that Mr. Beara was a familiar person. Where did he meet him before that? So there are two explanations of this events, either Mr. Beara was not familiar, or if he maintains he was familiar, then the viewing conditions must have been very bad, which raises doubt about his entire further statement about what happened then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just to try to move it along, although we are approaching the break, I want to look at the next two witnesses with respect to this category of recognition. In the last section of your report on paragraph 11, you talk about -- and we're going to come back to it, so I'm not going to take it out of context, but I want to just get a flavour for why and how you give this opinion. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before a Court accept the statements by a witness, it must be established whether these witnesses are not mistaken or are not lying. Both things can happen. Now, if a person claims to have seen the accused somewhere whereas in fact he never saw the accused, then he will not be able to pass the lineup test. So the lineup test is a very useful instrument to test whether the witnesses are mistaken or lying. That's what it is for. Now, with familiar persons you cannot apply the lineup test, and so from their recognition, you cannot infer that also the problem of possibly being mistaken or possibly lying is resolved, and that's why it is here. They may later on in photo boards -- in photos and pictures say, yes, that's the person I saw. But that's easy for them because it's a familiar person. And the question whether they are mistaken about who they saw when they encountered someone or even are lying about it is not resolved by that recognition. And the significance of that is that there must be other evidence to support the notion that they really met the person they described. Now, logically you can make a distinction between witnesses who can't be mistaken because it was very clear what they saw and witnesses who might be mistaken because it wasn't so clear what they saw. Now, Mr. Babic is an example of he might easily be mistaken because he isn't sure he saw Mr. Beara. So that's a clear example of where that question remained open. About the other two, I can only say --

utterances.text: Okay. And now we were going to --

utterances.text: And we were looking, Professor, at 2D602, which were photographs that I presented to you, and they depict Mr. Beara, and we'll go through them just quickly in the interest of time. utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe while we are waiting I can say something about showing photographs that might be helpful?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Court -- we gave, I think, the originals to the Court officer, and we don't have a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you may --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness was inquiring as to whether or not he can say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, Professor, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The showing of photographs one after another all in a particular context is in itself a suggestive procedure because it suggests you can see the same person in all photographs. utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not -- please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if that detailed information is not available, it's very hard to judge what the meaning is if a later statement says he recognised some or people in all -- even in all photographs. It depends, say, on the order in which they were presented.

utterances.text: And I'm just going to go through these photographs and as we see them, there, again, on the left-hand side, the gentleman with the glasses is Mr. Beara, and if we can go to the next photograph, please. utterances.text: Correct. If we can go to the next photograph, please. Do you remember being shown this photograph, sir?

utterances.text: And can you tell us what if anything is significant about this photograph, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's go to the next photograph, if we may, please. This is a photograph that's a family photograph, and I'm just going to tell you that it was after 1995, and we can see looking at the photograph, the second from the right is Mr. Beara. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]

utterances.text: And I think we all know, Professor, that Mr. Erdemovic in this photograph did not identify Mr. Beara as the person he purported to see in the site that he was at, and I know we have your testimony in connection with whether this photograph is highly suggestive or not. utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]

utterances.text: Yes, we were going to raise this even before in relation to some other questions, but here we have definitely a case of where the witness, Erdemovic, being shown this photo failed to recognise Beara. So what's the point of the whole exercise, question?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have in your section -- on your last section glasses and the significance of the description of appearance, and you highlight glasses. Let's go through some of this specifically with respect to witnesses which we have as PW 165, which in your report you identify under the number 135; witness who you identify as 113 whose name is Celanovic; and Witness number 21 who we briefly discussed today which was Egbers; and Witness 157 which we've identified as PW 104.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us your opinion in connection with those four witnesses, the relevance of their testimony in connection with eyeglasses.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. These four witnesses actually made a statement about glasses. They said that the person they saw did not wear glasses or did not continually wear glasses, so that's different from the last witness we discussed where it's uncertain whether it's just that he failed to mention it. This is a much positive -- much more positive statement about glasses. They didn't see it, or he was not wearing it continually. And that would be a significant piece of information in the context of more information about Mr. Beara's habits of wearing glasses, of which, of course, I'm not an expert. I can only say that the connection between these statements and the actual fact whether or not he always wore glasses, that connection is, of course, extremely relevant. If he wore always glasses, the question is, of course - and that's more in my field - would it be possible for people to not remember those glasses? And in principle, one can say everything can be forgotten, but not all people will forget everything. The fact that four witnesses say that there were not glasses or not always glasses is, in the context of how difficult it would be to remember that, would be quite surprising if in fact they always saw those glasses. utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor, Mr. President asked the question with respect to this photograph, and although we always like to do this compare and contrast, what I'd like to do is to show you a photograph of the video that Mr. Egbers was shown the seven or eight times, and I showed it my learned friend, and we're going to mark that, although it's not in e-court, because the video is -- it's 2D605, because I'd like your opinion to know if this video, although it's this snapshot in particular, that was the only time Mr. Beara purports to be there, whether this is suggestive, if the Court permits. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If necessary, we have it, and why don't we show it since they've raised an objection or an issue with that regard. May we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, we're going to show you the video that was shown to Mr. Egbers in a moment, and I just want you to focus on a number of factors in connection with that video, and I know that you've read Mr. Egbers' testimony in that regard, and I just have a few follow-up questions, so just please bear with us. For the Court and others, the video has been marked I think previously, and we'll get the Court that specific number. If we can just roll back a little bit to --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- I think, to rewind it. Can we rewind it? Yes, that's great. We can keep playing it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, the video goes on other issues that I think my learned friend will agree that other than for this segment, I don't believe what purports to be the gentleman Mr. Beara, nowhere else is it in the video, and I'll stand to be corrected on this, but I think I'm accurate on it. But would that be considered a suggestive way of helping someone recognise or identify a purported individual by showing him this video clip?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First thing is, of course, that this is definitely not the format that you would choose if you would present a formal identification test.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a number of reasons. There are only a few people there shown who feature prominently. They march in front of some bars, and there's a large crowd behind the bars. It would be totally unreasonable that a person you should identify would be one in the crowd behind those bars because that's clearly not visible at all. So any witness would conclude it's one of those people in the front I must recognise. That leaves, I think, three people, which is too small for a photo lineup anyway. These three people, they are wearing similar uniforms, but I can't say they fit the same description of the physical appearance, so it's logically impossible that two could be well-chosen foils for the third. That's the second reason -- third reason. The fourth reason is that in as far as the other persons are familiar to the witness, he could easily exclude the others on those grounds, which leaves only one candidate to be identified as the person who has been discussed. So those would be major deviations from the setup of a proper photo lineup test.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, despite those flaws or the opinions in connection with how this was shown to Egbers, do you have an opinion as to how many times the video should have been played in order to reasonably assess whether or not he can properly identify the individual he claims to have seen?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it very hard to answer that question because then I must guess at the objective of showing the video. To my mind, the objective cannot logically be that it would be for identification purposes because any investigator in the world knows that proper identification is done differently. What other objective there was, I can hardly guess. If it is believed when Egbers could not identify, say, one of those people, that repetition would help, then I can only say that the experience in person identification research is that if you are tested and you don't recognise anyone, repetition does not help.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when we discuss repetition in this particular case with this witness Egbers, was there repetition? I think you testified to it, but I don't want to lead you on this.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you show it seven to eight times, I would call that repetition. Recognition or identification do not become better, but another effect of repetition is, of course, that you increase the pressure. By repeating it seven to eight times you make it clear even without saying, you make it clear to the witness that this is important and that it really would be very helpful if he could identify anyone. And we know that pressure does not improve person perception, but it increases the tendency to guess. Now, in an exposition as this where logically you can come to some conclusion about whom actually is intended even without recognizing, pressure increasing the tendency to guess might lead to an apparent positive identification, whereas in fact, no one was actually recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Describe for me, if you will, in a typical situation where we have a proper photo identification board the person who is actually being tested, if you will, for recognition identification purposes. Not the creation of the board - we've discussed that - but actually the -- conducting that very test by presenting it to an individual for purposes of identification?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. In the instructions to a witness --

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it relates specifically to this video that they've shown and to give a witness an opportunity seven to eight times, I think it's critical without sharing, although I think we know what his answer is, and my learned friend certainly has read and knows the standard, but I think it's -- even with a photo board that is proper, I think it's important for us to know whether or not you would have a witness look at it on seven to eight different instances, which will ultimately be the follow-up question after we lay the foundation in connection with a proper photo board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You are a hundred-percent right, Mr. Nicholls, as it relates to Beara. However, the question might relate, also, to other of the accused for whom this procedure, photo board was used. So we are allowing the question only because of that and not because it has any relevance in the case of accused Beara. Did you get the gist of it, Professor? If you could answer, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour. In the proper photo board procedure, witnesses are instructed that they should not guess; they should only point at someone if they recognise a person immediately, which means that the actual recognition -- identification test last very short. You do not allow witnesses to look and look and look again, and it takes 10, 15 minutes. That's not immediate recognition. So usually it's done within a minute or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why is that significant, not to have him see it for a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because if there's no immediate identification, then a prolonged exposition increases the tendency to guess, and you don't want the witnesses to guess in identity questions because in the proper lineup of, say, eight photographs as it has been used in this Tribunal before still leaves a guessing tendency of one in seven. Now, one of seven is still a considerable risk, and the last thing you want to do is witnesses to guess. Photo confrontations are so particularly good because -- not because the guessing level is low, because it's not even so low, but because it discourages witnesses to guess because by seeing all these pictures, they realise, oh, my Lord, I'm not sure, and they only realise it when they see the photo board, and then they refrain from guessing. They refrain from pointing at anyone. That's exactly what you want. You want them to take the safe choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions with respect to Mr. Egbers. Last week we were given a document, which I think is identified as an information sheet for the first time, that relates to a witness called Theo Lutke, but in that information sheet, it also references Mr. Egbers. utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's not so clear on my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah, nor on mine.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Now it's getting better. Yeah. You want to draw my attention to a particular section of this document?
