utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can move --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- for any of the accused if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's move on. Yes, Professor. It's on the record in any case, Mr. Nicholls, so you don't have to worry about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I was -- if I can go back to the issue that I was trying to draw your attention to, and that's specifically Mr. Peric and 131. I just want to focus on it. utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. In his statement, he said he saw a group of people and one of them was a high-ranking older person, and he saw this group at a distance of 50 metres. I noticed that was an exclamation mark in my notes because 50 metres is of course much longer than the criterion of 20 metres that I found in my research beyond which the perception of people's faces becomes risky. 50 metres is such a long distance that accepting his testimony that -- whom he saw would be extremely risky without further testing. I would like to the Tribunal to stress again that such questions can be -- in principle be solved with a proper lineup testing. If he did see his face and remembered it, that would be revealed by a proper lineup test. Unfortunately, this witness stated that maybe he saw later pictures of Mr. Beara in the media. That excludes him as a witness who can be tested in a lineup. It doesn't exclude him as a witness, of course, but whom he saw cannot be tested in a lineup because if he saw pictures of Mr. Beara later, through unconscious transference he might be able to identify him in the photo board.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I just have one other -- a couple other items I'd like to cover with you, although we know how long it takes to create such a photo identification board and we know that the Prosecution has shown videos to the witnesses in the manner in which you've described. I want to show you a video that purports to be from a -- as we've identified, the Zivanovic party, and it is 2D596.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Mr. President, it's approximately 16 seconds of video clip that I'd like to show the witness for the purposes of my next several questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, as this is getting uploaded, I think you remember the video I'm referring to, right?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. For the record, we'd like to go to 41 minutes and 20 seconds and play it through 41 minutes and 36 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can we stop, please. Thank you. I've asked to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to focus on the gentleman which we cannot see, but we certainly see a portion of his -- back of his head, his ear, and that's the third gentleman when we look at the picture from his left, and now we lost that, but that's okay. utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then just so we have the correct time. We're going a little fast, but that's okay. Obviously, this gentleman here fits some of the descriptions that you've heard from the witnesses, from the testimony and statements that you've reviewed, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it's an elderly person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Professor. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to the leading. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic. Can you rephrase the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will. I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you could have put it the way you are rephrasing it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In this still, if you will, of a video that we have, do any of these three individuals fit the general description that was provided of the 12 witnesses that you've reviewed in connection with this case?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person on the right in this still fits the description of an elderly person with glasses. I cannot tell whether he is strongly built as some witnesses described Mr. Beara, nor can I see his insignia to see whether he's a lieutenant-colonel or colonel. The two others -- the one to the left might be described as having greyish hair; the person in the middle, clearly not; and the other two don't have -- don't wear glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can proceed with the film, then I'll ask you when to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we could fast forward to the section where the gentleman that we just saw was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in any event, Professor, let me just try to -- in the interest of time, we've seen that the Prosecution has taken from videos certain still shots like the exhibits that you've looked at specifically as it relates to Mr. Babic and his testimony. Would this type of video and capturing this person, for example, would it be -- and I know you don't want to talk about all the foils, but would this be a way to capture someone and place it on a foil for purposes of a photo board identification?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not the way it's usually done. Photo boards are usually compiled from clear photographs of people all taken in the same position, all wearing same uniform. I think if -- these images are not very clear, and especially if you reduce them to still they get worse, so no, I don't think this is very useful. In the case of Mr. Beara, which is the only case I study, of course, the situation is that at the time when the investigation started clear pictures of Mr. Beara were -- could have been used, and clear pictures of foils would even be easier to produce. And it's important that a photo board has a good quality and is not vague or shows unwanted differences because they are taken, had to be taken from poor available material.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Professor. My name is Zoran Zivanovic. I am representing Mr. Vujadin Popovic in this case. I was planning to put more questions to you, but a lot of them have already been covered now by my learned friend Mr. Ostojic so that my examination will be shorter. During your testimony, you indicated the difference between identification and recognition, and you explained -- actually, I would like you to clarify that part, and my questions will relate to that which relates to identification, so the recollection of the witness about the appearance of the person that he doesn't in fact know. I'm actually going to ask you, you spoke about the significance of the perception of the witness of a person at the site, whether the person is facing forward, to the side, et cetera. So my question will relate to the reliability of the identification of the person who is -- has their back turned to the camera. I would like you to ask a -- to look at a photograph. This is photograph P2324. It's from the Prosecutor's collection, which was used here. You can see two people in this photograph. One person is facing the camera. I'm not going to put any questions to you about that person. The other person is turned with their back or is seen from the side, but the head is turned or, actually, the face you cannot see. Now, I would like to ask you to tell us in your expert opinion how reliable the identification is that a witness would perform in relation to this person that has their back to us, that is on the right-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I can answer your question, I think I need a clarification. Is the witness you were mentioning identifying a person from this photograph? So the witness is not actually taking part in this scene; he's not present in this village?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely, Professor. The witness is carrying out an identification of this person that has their back turned on the basis of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The answer to your question is that an identification of this person might be misleading. It is -- it can be imagined that a witness would be able to say who this person is not. It's clearly not me, and it is not you, and it's a number of people not. Now, if the witness is in a situation where he realises that this can be only one out of a few persons, then he can reason logically that most people out of the group can be excluded because they look different even from the back. Then his logical conclusion might be, it can only be one person. But a logical conclusion is not the same as a direct perception, and in most cases, you as lawyers do not want witnesses to draw conclusions. They should report about their own experiences; and therefore, under certain conditions it should not be allowed to ask witnesses to identify such a person because it would encourage making inferences instead of reporting about the witness's direct experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would just like to ask you one other thing. Can you tell me something about the effect on the identification that passage of time has, the time from the day when the witness noticed a person until the day that he is called upon to identify that person on the basis of a photograph that is shown to him?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The time between perceiving a person and identifying him on the photograph can be very long even without loss of accuracy. It all depends what happened in that time. Some things are remembered over long periods of time because, one, they were very important to you, you paid a lot of attention to it; and two, you were thinking about it all the time because you were reminded to it all the time through over events in your life. We call that refreshment of memory. If life itself makes you, encourages you to refresh your memory, you can remember things, also images, for a long period of time. That would be good. But there's another effect. In a long period of time, you might receive new information, different information, which conflicts with your original memories. That information can also be pictorial, which is, you receive conflicting images. And the longer the time, the more opportunities there are for conflicting information, which is a negative influence on memory because memory has a tendency to integrate all information and build one coherent representation of the events that you experienced. So a long time might be very destructive on your memory if much conflicting information was received. Now, this means, in one short sentence, that the length of time per se is not very -- not very informative aspect of it. What is important is what happened in that time, either did you refresh your memories and kept them clear, or did you receive lots of conflicting information, and did your memories get distorted over time? Both is possible, and what you really want to know is not how long was the time but what happened in that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I just have one more question. How would you assess the reliability of identification if, for example, five years after the fact the witness would demonstrate uncertainty about the identification of a certain person but then in five more years spoke with a greater degree of certainty that that is the person involved?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that you're talking about speaking about identification without being tested in a formal lineup procedure, because that can be done only once, cannot be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. It's not that manner of identification. It's about identification that would be carried out five years after the fact and then another one that would be repeated five years more after the fact, in total, ten years after the event.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I understand your question, but one general piece of knowledge that we all have is that usually memory gets worse over time and does not get better, and that's also true for witnesses. Now, confidence in your memory is a totally different thing, and there is not much of a relationship between the accuracy of your memory and the confidence that you have in your memory. Now, the experience is that in time accuracy tends to go down and confidence sometimes goes up, so the discrepancy between what you actually remember and how confident you are becomes bigger and bigger. One of my students has just concluded her dissertation that she will defend this season in Leiden on exactly this problem, so I'm quite familiar with it, and what you are referring is not that identification has become better over the period of ten years because we cannot know that. You are describing that the confidence increased, which does not surprise me. But the general lesson is that although you might accept the memories of witnesses, do not equally easily accept their confidence in their memories because they might be totally wrong there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Bourgon, you had asked for one hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I had the opportunity of saying, I should be shorter, no more than 30 minutes, probably less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. If you could conclude by the break, that's fantastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We'll do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: For the record, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and I represent along with my colleagues today Drago Nikolic in these proceedings. Before I begin, I'd like you to confirm that we did have the opportunity of meeting last week. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I thank you very much for taking the time to meet me last week, and I will move --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel and witnesses are kindly asked to make pauses between questions and answers for interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise. Will do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will move to my first question, Professor, and -- which has to do with your report, which I read with much interest, and I refer here to part 2, section 5, of your report, which deals with description of appearance. And in that section, you refer to the literature on person description after a considerable retention interval. You've already answered a few questions to my colleague on this topic - I'm talking about Mr. Zivanovic - but I understand that this is part of your science; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'd like to obtain your assistance regarding the factors that will influence the memory of a witness or, let's say, what a witness will remember after a significant time lapse concerning the physical appearance and the characteristics of a person encountered only once. So in other words, my question is the following: If a witness is involved in a significant event, and not necessarily a crime but something significant, during which he or she meets a single person for the first time, and let's say that this person does not see -- the witness, sorry, does not see that person again for a considerable lapse of time - let's say seven years - what I would like to know is, from a scientific point of view, what is the witness likely to remember about the physical appearance and characteristics of the person?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe, first, it would be good to make clear that I can answer only your general questions about my science and that I have no knowledge whatsoever of the case of your client, so my answers really must be taken as general scientific answers. When we look at descriptions that people give of other people they have met in the past, then you see that when time lapses these descriptions become poorer and poorer; details get lost. And usually what people can explain spontaneously are very rough categories, for instance, male or female; they will remember what they saw. Caucasian or non-Caucasian or black or rough categories like Asian, they will remember. Some very general information about height; it was a very big person, a very small person. If there's nothing conspicuous there, they will probably not even mention it. They will remember very young or very old, so very rough, broad categories. And then the one issue that they find the easiest to remember about outer appearance is hair-do: bald, very long hair, very dark, curly hair, as in my case, lots of white hair. So hair-do is an important -- remains an important feature of the memories. Rather surprisingly, usually beards and moustaches get often lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. And what could we say about clothing?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clothing is very difficult unless it was highly conspicuous. Like, if you remember Santa Claus, you would remember, also, his clothing; but in wartimes, for instance, people seem to remember something like uniforms, but that could be any type of uniforms, and they get easily confused about the uniforms. Some of my research is on remembering uniforms in concentration camps, in German concentration camps, and what we know from survivors of concentration camps, that they're often totally wrong on the uniforms they attribute to certain people. And I should warn you, they are not wrong about uniforms they saw; they are wrong about which person wore which uniform. And that's, of course, the essential information that the Court needs to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My next question is, I would like to take a practical example, of course, without going into the facts of this case, and I would simply ask that if a witness saw you today for the first time as you testify in this significant trial and that person does not see you again for a period of seven years, if this person was asked to describe your physical appearance, what is he or she likely to remember about your physical appearance and characteristics?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That witness will probably remember that I'm male, I'm Caucasian, I'm an elderly person, I have white hair, and then it depends on whether the witness saw me sitting here behind the stand because then nothing about length or build could be said, or whether the witness saw me walk. If the witness saw me walk, probably nothing very special would be remembered. I'm not extremely fat; I'm definitely not extremely thin; I'm not extremely tall, not extremely small. There's nothing really that would strike the witness in such a way that could be remembered after seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, it's twice now that you mentioned -- first, you said a lot of white hair spontaneously before I asked that question, and now you mention again the white hair. Just how important is the white hair concerning you personally?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understand your question. It's something people will remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and whether it's important to anyone, I'm not so certain, apart for myself and my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me be more precise, Professor. That witness who saw you only once today and describes you seven years from now, how important or how is it likely that he or she will remember the white hair?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's -- of all my general features, it's the most likely thing that would be remembered.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, again, without going into the facts of this case, if white hair and hair-do is a significant characteristics, if I add to this a person who is young - let's say 30, 35 - with white hair and a specific hair-do, how important would that be in describing this person seven years down the road?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that depends on -- in itself, it is remarkable that a young person would have completely white hair; also, I myself did. But whether that would strike a witness as special depends on whether the witness can estimate the age of that person. If for other reasons it would be clear to the witness that this is a very young person, the witness would think, this is odd, and that would make it even more likely that the white hair would be remembered. But in general, of course, the estimation of age is in part dependent upon the colour of the hair. So it's also possible that your hypothetical witness would be mistaken about the age as seeing nothing special. So it's one of the two, and how this must be applied to your case, of course, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, again, I don't want to get into the specifics of the case, but if the person does recognise that person or does recognise person as being a young person having white hair, would you agree that this would be a significant detail?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the witness would be able to realise this is a very young person, it would strike him as -- it would draw his attention that young person had white hair. That makes it even more likely to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. My understanding, also, is that you referred to other factors which influence the quality or the precision of a person's recollection, and I'd like to look at a couple of them. The first one you discussed briefly with my colleague Mr. Zivanovic, and that is the retention period. You've covered that already. My question here will be quite specific. What if the retention period is cut in half by a second encounter? Let's say the period of seven years I mentioned was cut in half because the witness saw the person again after three or four years. What would be the effect?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The effect of a second meeting, that would be a good example of what I called refreshment. Now that memory is refreshed. I assume that the person in the meantime has not significantly changed because then we cannot talk about refreshing an old memory because then we must talk about producing a new memory. After your meeting halfway, see, the forgetting process starts again in principle, but now the forgetting period is only if it was after -- of the seven halfway, it's only three and a half years instead of seven. The forgetting curve really is measured from the last encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The next criteria I would like to look at is the emotional significance of the encounter. How would that play a part in whether a witness was able to recognise seven years down the road a person he met only once?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship between emotions and the quality of memory is very complex because there are two effects. One is that emotions make memory worse, and the other is that emotions make memory better. And to make a very complex matter -- to simplify it a little bit, one of the determining factors is the fact that emotions at a certain moment narrow the field of your attention. You pay more attention to some important things but less attention to the other things, and so -- and the things you paid more attention to will also be remembered better, but that is at the cost of the things you now paid less attention to because they will remember it worse. So the question about emotions cannot be answered if it is not first addressed whether the thing that needed to be remembered or the thing that is reported later can be assumed to be something to which all your attention went during the emotion or that it would be something that would in fact be cut out of your attention because it was less important. And the answer to what actually will happen can only be determined on the basis of an exact description of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. The next criteria I would like to quickly look into, and you've touched already a bit on it, is an opportunity to remind. So the witness had a reason to think about the event during the period of seven years. Would that be important?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be an example of what I called refreshment, things you are reminded to just -- spontaneously or through events in your lifetime are better remembered than things you never thought about and suddenly after many years are recovered in your memory again. So refreshment of memory is very much related to the degree to which you are reminded to these events. But I must warn you there. If you are reminded just because that's how life goes, that's different from being reminded to it through conflicting information because conflicting information may worsen your memory. Just being reminded because like in the war, having survived a war, everything around you reminds you to that war all the time, it's not something that will move away and will move out of your life. So that type of reminding would refresh your memory all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I only have two more questions, Professor. The first one is, one of the things you mentioned when we met is that an event -- the more important the event, the more likely it will be burned in the memory, and you refer to something that an event burned in the memory usually comes with a picture. Can you explain that for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, memory is about facts, but some aspects of memory are pictorial. We can describe actually what things looked like, and we can also -- we call that imagery. You can close your eyes and try to see that picture in front of you and even describe it then. And some events that do not constitute general knowledge but constitute events, things that you have seen may be remembered not only in terms of words or a story or facts but also in a pictorial manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to a colleague -- question by my colleague representing the accused Beara, you referred to a rule of plus or minus 5 that you personally use, and if I sum up your conclusion is that anything over 10, plus or minus 10, in terms of kilos, age, or height in centimetres, that this leads to the conclusion that the witness either does not remember or never met the person. Is that a summary of your answer to my colleague's question?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. That's far too strong. What I said is below 10, you should not be surprised if that happens. Above 10 -- and you are quite right. This is only true in the metrical world. We are talking about centimetres and kilograms, not about inches and pounds. Above 10, my experience is it's very wise to raise the hypothesis whether this is really the person that the witness thinks he or she met. I didn't say it's proven that he met another person or it's impossible he met this person. I think it becomes a reasonable thing to test because it's a good reason to have doubt, but doubt is not the same as definite proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question, Professor, is the following: Coming back to the example using yourself and the description -- your physical description, if a witness who claims to have seen you seven years ago was asked to describe you today and omitted entirely the white hair, based on your scientific knowledge would you conclude that this description is unreliable?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are various steps. Step one is that you ask a witness to produce a spontaneous description. That's important in any interrogation; and the spontaneously reproduced description, that's the most important part of the evidence. Usually, witnesses produce a description of hair-do spontaneously. If they don't, there are two possible reasons: One is they don't remember that, so they didn't tell you; and the other is they didn't think that was important and, therefore, didn't say it. You can test that thing by asking for more descriptives without saying hair-do. If they forgot hair do, if you just ask anything else, what more, and they remember their hair, they're most likely to say it. If they still don't mention hair, you can ask them a directed question: What about their -- do you remember the hair? That's already a little bit suggestive because now you draw the attention to a certain thing and you put some pressure on them to tell something about the hair. But as long as it is known to the Court that this question was asked, the Court can take that also into account. Nothing about hair in take one; nothing about hair in take two; only after directed question, that's weaker. That represents a lower level of reliability. If the person then says, yes, he had bright red hair, you know he's talking about someone else. If he still at a direct question cannot reproduce the white hair, that's very strong evidence because he's got all the chances, even part of a suggestion that he should say something like that. So it is a complicated matter, how to evaluate what people say about hair-do. Important is for all that it's properly reported how the interrogation exactly went and whether the interrogator followed this -- the professional standard of first spontaneous, then another attempt at A spontaneous declaration, then a directed question with the question recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. I have no other question. Mr. President, I finished before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well done, Mr. Bourgon. We'll have a 25-minute break. And how long do you think your cross-examination will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it will be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it will be less than my estimate, which I think was three hours, but not dramatically less. I mean, I think I may cut it down to 2, 2 and a half, something like that. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you so much. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before I ask you, Mr. Lazarevic, if you wish to cross-examine this witness, the other Defence teams and Prosecution, we need roughly five minutes towards the end to discuss something, housekeeping matters, all right? Thank you. And if you think we need more particularly, Mr. Ostojic, you and Mr. Bourgon in particular, because you are the two who are most directly involved in what we are going to say, tell us and we'll reserve more than five minutes. Yes. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Surprisingly, Mr. President, it's me today, and we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau, s'il vous plait.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, Madam. Mr. Josse, you definitely have because we've seen the documents that you are going to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Professor Wagenaar, my name is Josse. I'm one of the Defence counsel for General Milan Gvero. It's right that you and I have never met, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's also right that you have not discussed General Gvero's case with the best of our knowledge with anyone?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so you have no idea what I'm going to ask you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to clarify something. As you will gather in a few moments' time, what I'm interested in is recognition, and you talked at some length about recognition this morning, and in the course of your testimony at about page 11 of today's transcript, you also started to talk about height and weight issues, talking about 5 centimetres on, off, so on and so forth. That refers to identification issues only, I assume; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. What I said is if people are asked to describe a person they met, if they give particulars with respect to height, age, weight, they might be so many measures off, and that refers both to familiar people and unfamiliar people. It's on the basis of having met and their perceptions during this encounter. It would only be different if a familiar person is so familiar that you didn't estimate those things because you know them. Of my own family, I know their age; I don't have to estimate it, so that's different. But if there are familiar people like people here in the courtroom who I have now seen and in a later encounter would be counted as familiar because I've seen them before, of no one here in the courtroom I know the height or the age or their weight, so I still would have to estimate that. I'm referring to these estimates, and these estimates can be about familiar people and unfamiliar people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So like so much of your evidence, it's matter of extent and degree, the extent and degree to which the witness knew the suspect prior to the alleged encounter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There is some extent of familiarity where one would simply know about one another how tall they are or how much we weigh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But in a situation where the witness and the suspect did not know each other particularly well, what you're saying is it would be a prudent question to ask of the witness, what was the height of the suspect, what was his age, what was his weight, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, and then it should also be prudent so ask, do you know this or did you estimate them, because my rules apply to the situation where it was estimated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And at what juncture do you say it would be prudent to ask those type of questions, in court or prior to court in the course of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule is always that you ask questions as soon as is possible because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think here we're veering away from expertise in memory, recognition, and into investigative techniques, and I'm not sure that's -- not really part of his field of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse, would you like to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, I radically disagree bearing in mind the range and extent to which this witness has testified hitherto, I suggest my question was perfectly permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please answer the question. We agree entirely with Mr. Josse on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect to the aspect of forgetting, it's always wise to ask questions as soon as is possible, and if a case is investigated a long time before it comes to court, it would be very wise to have asked relevant questions during the investigation and not to wait until witnesses appear in court. This is especially true with their memories to physical appearance of people, which is very much dependent on pictorial representations more than a factual memory because those are not facts they can remember. It's something they have to estimate, and probably they will do the estimation when the question is asked and not before; and therefore, it's urgent to ask this question as soon as is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to a slightly different topic, and in this regard could we please have in e-court 2D590. And specifically, it's page 11 at the bottom that I would like. Now, whilst this is being brought up, this is an extract from an unpublished article that you have written headed "Expert Witness In International War Crimes Tribunals." And beyond this particular table, I'm not going to ask you anything to do with this article, but you produced this table as some sort of guide and help in relation to recognition situations. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I hope you won't take this the wrong way, but much of what you have put here is no more than common sense, isn't it, as to what a tribunal of fact should take into account in assessing the reliability of a purported recognition witness, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're partially correct because some of the items mentioned here are only relevant because you can fall back on the research that we have done on those things. So for instance, I mentioned distance and illumination there. I wouldn't have if in the scientific knowledge body there is not sufficient information about what -- how distance and illumination [Realtime transcript read in error, "elimination"] should actually be used. So it's only partly -- it's only --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me interrupt you at this point.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only partly common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you at this point. It's the same issue again. It's illumination, not elimination, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, illumination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Same issue we had --

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it correct in the page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it's line 7, it's incorrect. Let me go on. This list is not exhaustive, is it? For example, would you agree that the concentration that the witness had both in the course of the prior recognition and also at the scene of the alleged crime is a factor that a Court might want to take into account?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whether the witness had been distracted in either of the two encounters, correct?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so there are issues here that are of assistance, but as I've already said, there are certain categories that one could add to the list?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on from that, please, and ask if a particular document could be placed on the ELMO. Could I hand this to the usher. This is an extract from an English criminal law textbook, the leading textbook on English criminal law, which is called Archbold. It's from the 2007 edition published by Sweet and Maxwell, and it's page 1487, and we can see at the top it's dealing with visual identification. And in the middle of the page, perhaps it could be -- up a little bit, please, because it's the middle paragraph 14/19 that I'm interested in. That's perfect. Thank you. We can see that it deals with identification of strangers and recognition. Now, what this book purports to do is set out a rough guide as to what a judge should remind a jury of in the course of his or her summing up as to the type of factors they may wish to take into account in a recognition case, and I want to ask you going through these one by one from your scientific perspective whether you agree with these and whether you can comment upon them. So it says, summarising the first three lines, that the fact of the recognition rather than identification case doesn't absolve the Judge from giving this type of direction, and it cites a variety of cases, and then it says that in the 1991 case called Bentley, Lord Lane, then-chief justice, "... observed that recognition evidence could not be regarded as trouble-free. Many people had experienced seeing someone in the street whom they knew only to discover they were wrong. The expression ' I could have sworn it was you ' indicated the sort of warning a judge should give because that was exactly what a witness did: He swore it was the person he thought it was." Stopping there, can you comment on that, please?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have a question about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, my question is, do you think that a tribunal of fact should take that into account from your scientific perspective in assessing whether a recognition is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's the kind of statement I would like to make. I can only say that what is summarized here is an agreement with my own positions, and what the Tribunal needs to take into account in a particular case I think should be decided by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go on and deal with it this way. Let's read on a bit: "In the narrow field of recognition there were degrees of danger, perhaps less so where the parties had known each other for many years or where the person identified was at the scene." And I assume that the author there means it's accepted that the person identified was at the scene --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel is kindly asked to read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That falls full square in agreement with what you have testified hitherto. Isn't that right, Professor?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Recognition and identification are never guaranteed to be correct, and that's why in our scientific discipline the stress is very much on how do we test? How can we help Courts to test claims about identification and recognition? What are the best possible method we can contribute that can be used by investigators and finally by the Court to test whether this sort of error has occurred or not? And that's always under the assumption that there's always a possibility that recognitions and identifications are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you have already commented, haven't you, that it's very difficult if not impossible for you to assess whether any particular witness making a purported identification is lying or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will never say that a witness is lying. It's not my discipline to make out whether someone is lying. There even is -- doesn't exist a good scientific method to determine whether someone is lying, so that would simply not be within my discipline. I also will never say that a recognition or an -- a specific recognition or identification was correct or wrong. I can only make an evaluation of the criteria and the methods that were used by legal parties to give an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because, of course, it's for the tribunal of fact to decide whether the witness is accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we can see, just reading on one more sentence, that the direction that I'm asking you -- the legal direction that I'm asking you to comment upon really postulates that one is dealing with an honest mistake because it says: "Even here, it's visible to alert the jury to the possibility of honest mistake and to the dangers and the reasons why such dangers exist in identification evidence." And really, the reason I've asked you these questions is to draw a distinction between the possibility of an honest mistake and the possibility of a deliberate deception from the witness.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously it's my opinion that since a recognition or an identification is never a hundred-percent certain to be correct, courts and juries, find the fact, should address that problem and be reminded to that problem. Nothing against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The problem of miscarriages of justice based on a wrongful honest identification, in other words where the witness is telling the truth, so he or she thinks, but it is in fact mistaken or may be mistaken, that's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, although I would like to add that there is a relationship between mistakes by witnesses and the quality of the procedures used when they were tested, and the attention of court and juries should not simply be addressed to the possibilities that witnesses are wrong but should be addressed at making an assessment of the witness statements through an assessment of the testing procedures that were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The document that I have just shown you is going to be in e-court as 6D307, let me say for the record. Now, turning back if we may for one brief moment to the document that was in e-court before - that is 2D590, page 11 - I want to ask you a little bit more about lapse of time. You've been asked a number of questions about lapse of time by both my learned friend Mr. Zivanovic and Mr. Bourgon, and I'm going to ask you a specific situation, and if you are unable to help, do say so, please. But in a scenario where the witness accepts that from the point of his recognition of the witness at the crime scene to the point in which he first mentions it to either an investigator or someone else a period of 12 years elapses, can you comment on the specifics of that situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I -- first of all, one, the witness doesn't have the specifics. Two, it's a question, unless I'm reading it wrong, which the witness cannot possibly -- this witness could not possibly answer because in the fact pattern posed, the witness would need to know what was in the mind of the person who did not mention this point for 12 years, and there could be any myriad of reasons why, so I think it - sorry for this long objection - it calls just for gross speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the Prosecution really don't want me to put my case, then I'll withdraw the question. I've got no real difficulty with that. Sorry. Too fast. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Archbold would tell you to take it more philosophically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nice deep breath. Yes. I apologise to the interpreters, but I repeat what I say. If my learned friend really doesn't want me to ask that question, then I won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. The presumption is that you as an expert in the field know for yourself whether you can answer this question or not. If you can answer it, please, go ahead. If you can't, just tell us, and we'll proceed with Mr. Josse's next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was just going to answer with the argument provided by the Prosecutor that there are thousands of reasons why people do not mention certain things. My specialty is in memory, and the assumption that it has to do with memory is not obvious to me, so I would find it very difficult to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can you comment - and only do so if it is within your sphere of expertise - as to how in your opinion it goes to reliability of the testimony of the witness?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean when a witness mentions a certain fact after a long interval of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends -- it depends totally on why the subject actually did not mention it before. It can be something that he always burned to tell but didn't dare or couldn't, never forgot it; on the contrary, remembered it better and better until finally after 12 years he could not withhold himself and finally came forward with it. That would be an example of a case where that information could be highly reliable. If on the contrary, as I meet in my practice quite often, subjects claim that they have totally forgotten this information or repressed it and then suddenly recalled it later in a dream or so therapy, I would call that testimony into question. So it really depends on the specifics of the case, and I would -- I can answer such a question related to your case after I've studied the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just -- I think finally this. You did say earlier at page 64, line 16 -- you were commenting on your student who it about to defend her dissertation at Leiden University. "The experience is that in time accuracy tends to go down and confidence sometimes goes up, so the discrepancy between what you actually remember and how confident you are becomes bigger and bigger."

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how does that fit in with what you have just said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about a general phenomenon that can be applied on specific instances only if these specific instances are well described. So although in -- generally it's true that the longer the elapsed time, the higher this discrepancy, not telling something that is relevant for 12 years is in itself a remarkable event, and the risk is far too high that that particular example simply doesn't fit with the general situation I described when I explained accuracy and confidence. So I would not simply apply that rule as a strict rule to just any situation, and I'm very much afraid of just explaining very broad and general principles of my discipline and leave it to various parties to apply that at will to their own case because there's risk that that application would be misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So is what you're saying, Professor, that in order for your testimony to have any validity you need to examine in detail each and every purported identification recognition and that what you testify about has very little general application?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, I said it has a high general value but can be misleading if it is applied to not only a specific but an exceptional case. The case you are describing reminds me to the possibility that this might be an exceptional case and that, therefore, general rules should not be too quickly -- not too quickly be applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. You're saying a court, a tribunal of fact, can apply your general principles so long as they, the tribunal of fact, is aware of the surrounding circumstances of the purported recognition?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the end the tribunal must apply any knowledge that I can transfer to this audience, and I think it's a safe assumption that the tribunal knowing all the facts of the case will do this in a sensible manner. But since I am not aware of all the facts of the case of your client, I would be reluctant to improvise on possible applications.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I quite understand. My apologies if I have put you on the spot, and in the circumstances, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Sarapa. Mr. Nicholls, we have 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Shall I go for five or ten, Your Honours? I'm just not sure. You said some time at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, you go for then. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm Julian Nicholls, and I'll be asking you some questions briefly today and for sure we'll finish tomorrow. Just to be clear, as Mr. Ostojic said, we met this morning for a few moments, and you kindly provided me -- both of us a couple of pages of your handwritten notes. And I reminded you that I -- although I hadn't cross-examined you I had actually been in the courtroom and observed your testimony in the Limaj trial, and just for your recollection, to be fair to you, I also met with you at your house before the Limaj trial with the Defence attorneys, and we discussed your testimony, in case I look familiar. My first question I've struck, because you just explained that very well, about your role and the role of the Court and who weighs the evidence ultimately. Before we finish today, I'd like to ask you a few questions about the different ways - and you touched on this - in the way the memory or the mind remembers faces from the way it remembers names, and I'll ask you in a minute also about refreshing. You've referred to visual memory earlier in your testimony here, and that's the way we remember faces, correct, as a picture? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that's not entirely right. The pictorial part is certainly important in remembering faces, but if I see someone who reminds me of my uncle, I can try to remember that face and I can also try to remember the fact that he looked a little bit like my uncle. In fact, I always tell police officers when you see people do things, try to verbalise what the person looks like because that verbal information is probably better recalled than the visual information. But it's also true that many witnesses cannot give you that sort of verbal information: I thought, hey, he looks like so-and-so, and then that's why I remember, or I thought, hey, what big glasses are those, that's why I remember it. So quite often it comes down to only having some pictorial memory, which they describe for the first time when they are interrogated. After interrogation, they have verbalized it, and that verbalisation becomes also part of the memory of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. I want to read you a little bit of your testimony in Kupreskic. This is from the 3rd of June, 1999. It was at page 94865 of that testimony. This is in e-court as 3663. I don't think we necessarily need to bring it up. And here's what you said about remembering faces and names: "Now, the problem with a face is that it's very difficult to refresh the picture of a face in your memory if you are not shown the picture, so if you have to remember the face of a bank robber, but they have not caught the culprit yet, so you're not confronted with that face, in the meantime the witness may forget the faces because they are not refreshed. But if you have to remember a name, you can refresh that yourself. Every time you tell the story, this is what happened to me, this person did that to me, the name is refreshed. It can happen several times a day, and there's no reason why memory would fade at all." Is that still a correct explanation? Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely, and I think it was in the context of a discussion about the difference between familiar and unfamiliar persons. If you see a familiar person do something, you don't have to remember the face of that person because you already know the face of that person. You only have to remember the name of the person you saw. Whereas if you see an unfamiliar person who is not named by any name to you, you have to remember the outer appearance until the investigation and you are shown photographs or something. So the memory processes involved in remembering familiar and unfamiliar people are entirely different, and the influences during time that might change or distort your memories are also different in those two situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But if I understood that correctly, as well, the ability to refresh a name is something that we can do ourselves without an external aid like a photograph, and that's just something in the way our minds work?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions now. You met with the Beara team I think we said in May 2007. I think I know this, but it was the Beara team who selected the 12 witnesses for you to review; is that correct? You didn't select those 12 witnesses out of the trial record?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was the team who selected the witnesses. I have no knowledge -- I received no documents about other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you had access to - as we've seen because my friend provided me with a record of that - transcripts as well as witness statements, in some cases, proofing notes, what we call them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you have access -- or did you request any other documentation, things like military reports, intercepts, physical evidence, anything else to try to put some context in the witness statements you were reading or the transcripts? In other words, you never said, all right, the witness is referring to an exhibit, I need to see that exhibit, something like that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I can put this straight. Whatever I asked to see I was always provided with. There was no information refused by the team, and what I actually have seen is in those -- is defined by the contents of those three binders that you have copied.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And once you got those three binders, did you in fact ever ask for any more information? Did you say I need this statement, I need from this witness, I need the earlier transcript, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not ask for documents of -- that I know existed. I sometimes expressed the desire that on some things there would have been more documentation, although I know it didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were also provided with sort of some summaries or -- yeah, summaries of the different testimony to kind of help you -- of the topics why these witnesses were called or selected?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think "I was provided with" is not the correct term. I prepared such summaries together with, as I said, Mr. Philip, the man who was the case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not simply fed by summaries that I had to use or so. That's not the way I work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And so with the case manager, you sat down and prepared the summaries?

utterances.speaker: WILLEM WAGENAAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This would be a good time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you, Professor. We'll meet you again tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That will be at 9 o'clock, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you, just like today. Mr. Ostojic, last week, Thursday, you remember that we had made it clear that today you were to come back and give us an exact date when your case would be laid to rest so that Mr. Bourgon who comes after you -- sorry, not Mr. Bourgon, the Nikolic Defence team that comes after you will know exactly when they should start or when they are expected to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Little did I know at the time that there would be developments as there have been. First of all, we knew at the time that the one would have been the next witness, the one for whom we had already set in place a videolink from Belgrade, has fallen through; you've withdrawn that witness because of reasons that you explained last time, but now it seems that the witness that you had intended to bring after him and in relation to whose testimony we had planned to have another videolink with -- somewhere else has approached you and specifically asked you to -- or informed you that he doesn't wish to give testimony as per your communication to us and his letter to you. So our first question to you is the following: Are you withdrawing that witness, too, or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We are preparing a written notice of withdrawal in connection with that witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, which brings us in this situation where of course I have to call upon Mr. Bourgon, Ms. Nikolic to tell us what the position would be because we will, I suppose, finish for sure with Professor Wagenaar tomorrow, but then do you have any other witnesses? You had mentioned the DutchBat guy, but I understand that he, too, is unavailable this week and don't know whether he will be available afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to the DutchBat individual, he will be available afterwards. He is on a mission in Germany as I think I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He can only meet with us later in the week. I think it was Thursday and Friday in the evening. It is two-plus hours away. I've been -- visited with him in the past. I hope to accomplish that this week. My thought was essentially to close my case when I've complete the evidence of the three remaining witnesses that I think we've identified and the Prosecution is aware of and then either seek leave or to determine how I can bring back this DutchBat individual, and I have been in discussions with my learned friends specifically in connection with the one exhibit that I think we've identified as 2D172, and it may have an impact on Captain Egbers' testimony, and we're still looking at that but didn't quite get the complete picture. The three remaining witnesses, if I may, outside of Professor Wagenaar is our expert Gogic who is here, and we are preparing him this evening and we will -- or hope to put him on after the testimony of Professor Wagenaar. I think all the parties are aware of that, and then following that we have two other witnesses that we will be calling. When we did the estimations based on the cross-examination estimates, although given this recent development over the weekend that the Court has referenced and made aware, we still believe we can finish our case now by Thursday given the estimates and if we all maintain those estimates as being accurate. So just so the Court is aware, for Mr. Gogic we have put down approximately two hours. The Prosecution has estimated one full hour, although it was a reduction from before, and I'm not sure if it's accurate. The remaining Defence estimates were approximately a half hour, which would lead us into a full day. With respect to the next witness, and I just have to check with these witnesses so I can't give you their names because I want to just make sure they are not going to be asking for any pseudonyms, the remainder two witnesses each were estimated by us to be one hour each on direct, and the Prosecution estimated one hour for each on cross or approximately that much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, which means, Ms. Nikolic and Mr. Bourgon, when can you start? Friday or Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. On Monday, Mr. President, the reason being that based on the information that we have, we contacted the victims and witnesses section, and our first group of witnesses will be arriving on Friday, so we'll be ready to go on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam registrar, we had asked your replacement last week or whenever it was to contact the Prlic Trial Chamber to shift these sittings -- to swap these sittings on Wednesday and Thursday. Wednesday and Thursday, yes, exactly. Now, we don't need to swap anymore now, so you could perhaps contact them and inform them that the reason which had prompted us to ask for our sittings, respective sittings to be swapped is no longer valid and that we would like to revert to the previous position. In other words, we will have the sitting in the morning and they will continue to have the sitting in the afternoon, all right? Thank you, and you will inform us of the outcome tomorrow morning. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Very quickly, there two pending matters that the Trial Chamber should be made aware of. First, of course, there is a motion we filed pursuant to rule 92 bis for one witness, 3DW26, but we haven't got a response from the Prosecution, and we're beyond the 14 days. The second matter is that we have a stipulation that we will be -- joint stipulation that we will be filing with the Prosecution. This is a matter that has been ongoing for quite some time, actually, even before the case with the Defence started, but we should be filing this this week. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you could perhaps let us know what your position is about the Nikolic motion for the addition of one witness. Thank you.
